title: Good AI for pixel art?
author: RelativeAd370
selftext:
I’m developing my game but want to add sprites to it. I’ve tried tier 1 (the 10$ one) of PixelLab but the MCP of it doesn’t work well with Godot MCP in Cursor. The way it generates things and implements them into the game doesn’t work well, all the tiles are messed up, resolutions are wrong and the art isn’t considered and doesn’t look that good.

Any help is appreciated 🙏

comments.author: proximalcoast
comments.body:
So as a one shot (it knows and works), it’s always gonna be bad. Even the wrappers that “fix it” will still do multiple iterations.

Your best bet is to understand the process. Do you know what it takes to make good pixel art in your genre? Stardew valley vs Super Mario have different requirements entirely. 

AI is a tool that only gets you so far. You have to understand the desired output and know what you need. Blindly asking and then integrating with no gates or review, I’d expect this to fail.

AI is only as good as the work you put into it.

replies.author: IwannagoCampn
replies.body:
I fully agree with your statement here. I myself am looking for a way to have AI pixelated art, yet I have failed MANY MANY times. I've had different skills taught to the AI with references to stardew valley, but still it gets it wrong. It makes a normal AI image, then seems to attempt to add the pixelated boxes to it. This has brought ALOT of inconsistencies in the sizes and layout of the pixels.

I like what you said about understanding the desired output. What area of the internet would you suggest to further ones education on the matter of pixel art and the fundamentals surrounding how it looks and feel?

replies.author: proximalcoast
replies.body:
It might be less about pixel art and more about just art in general. 

Blender can do vastly awesome pixel art through compositing, and the mcp is pretty good. I’ve not tried… yet, but it’s in the plans. There are some pretty good YouTube videos on this.

But understanding light/shadow, shot composition, color theory are all important. Cgcookie and blenderguru were my go-tos, but it’s been years. I think cgcookie is probably your best bet. They cover a lot of stuff. I only ever did what was free.

This is all AI (still working on the texture / uv map, as this is v2, I needed it to be chunkier), but knowing the terms (it started with two orbs and a cylinder, which is stupid), and then knowing how to UV unwrap makes the whole thing a lot easier and guidance simpler. The goal is to take all the feedback and to a better 1 shot for the future. Only 15-20 minutes of human work vs 2-3 hours of an agent. I could have modeled this myself already (probably), but I have like 40-50 to do, which would be impossible as a hobby

comments.author: RiffRuffer
comments.body:
I've also had this question and most of the options are mediocre at best. They all make okay stuff for like conceptualizing what you might want your art to look like but even the best output is gonna have mixels and weird artifacts.

The only time I've routinely got good results is telling an llm to make a python script that manually places down pixels one by one and generating images through that with a lot of constraints. Even with that I've only really been able to make things with very very low pixel counts without odd perspective and color issues. Anything more complex things get uncanny and weird.

In fact just today I tried to have fable 5 generate the last couple of sprites I need for a couple of enemies with a 16x16 canvas limit with the python script thing in claude cowork and while there's no mixels none of them look great and everything that implies motions is going to need heavy tweaks. The best stuff in my current project is either stuff I heavily tweaked or made from scratch.

If you want a pixel aesthetic I think doing it yourself with a low pixel count is your best bet. It's not gonna look amazing but if you're making a small prototype it's going to look a lot more cohesive then a bunch of nano banana stuff or whatever.

comments.author: machvelli
comments.body: Generate a schema so you can create your own sprites/backgrounds/foreground objects separately rather than procedurally generating them. Once you’ve created the assets, you can drop in and replace them to wire it up.

comments.author: Psychological-Key-36
comments.body: I’m a pixel artist and making good looking, adequate ai pixel art for my games is more tedious than actually doing the pixel art myself. And this should speak volumes because I’m normally lazy as fuck

comments.author: Varrianda
comments.body: Pixellab is the best tool for pixel art and it’s not very good. It’s workable, but it’s not “production quality”. That said, it’s actually pretty good for UI art

comments.author: woodysixer
comments.body: Check out [spritecook.ai](http://spritecook.ai) – Building stuff on their website is a bit awkward and confusing, with mixed results, but it does a great job when I have Claude Code use it via MCP for my Godot game.

comments.author: Immediate_Hornet8273
comments.body: I use PixelLab but developed my own python scripts that convert the zip packages or gifs into sprite sheets, then I use Upscayl to enhance them so they are less pixel(y) with an option in my game to use “HD” sprites, which creates a very cool look. I do have to say that PixelLab rendering has been very hit or miss, sometimes with one of the directions rendering a completely different looking or deformed sprite (or facing the wrong direction) and regenerating them doesn’t seem to fix it. It’s really inconsistent but I made it work for now.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
With the right prompt, any SotA AI can give you a good base for pixel art. GPT Image 2.0 is probably best. 

However YOU have to understand what makes good pixel art in order to prompt the appropriate color instructions for your game. You'll then have to either create an automated tool (or manually do it) to convert all mixels into pixels and palletize your pieces. THEN you'll want to go through any generated art and manually adjust pixels here and there with something like acesprite. Not every piece will need significant curation, but often times the mixel -> pixel conversion leaves certain shapes off.

If you're animating it, it gets trickier as you'd have to do that with each frame, then get an onion skin tool to let you view frames on top of each other. Depending on how high of quality you needed/wanted your animation, you'd want to then use that comparison to adjust pixels so that forms remain the same even as the pixels animate (this is why for small pixel art shapes it's best to just hand animate in a lot of cases. AI tends to fuck around with the pixels and they'll shift randomly, which is not how pixel art animation works. If a sword is a 3 pixels wide and 6 pixels long (the blade) with a single pixel at the top in the middle, then that sword should stay 3x6 (with the one on top). AI generated pixel animation will end up with that sword  shifting every single frame into a slightly different shape, and that will apply to the entire image. If you're talking high fidelity pixel art instead of more traditional 16x16, 32x32, etc, then you can get away with more pixel bleed. But at that point there's really no reason to even use pixel art IMO. Takes too long to do by hand and there's no retro payoff.

With a small 16x16 sprite, manually animating something like a hand waving a wand is extremely easy, and most of the time with pixel art, because you're trying to maintain the pixel forms, you aren't animating the entire thing anyway. Movements are isolated to draw the eye.

Another direction is the Hyper Light Drifter route where you have larger than traditional sprites, but a flat color palette with cel shading and large color blocks instead of more detailed shading and highlights, meaning though you're changing large swathes of pixels, those changes are easy to maintain and simple to paint in with a brush due to being fairly broad in stroke.

  
Regardless. If all that sounds like a lot of work, I suggest picking another style or focusing on just doing the static images without animations. Static images are easy enough to set up, though they require a bit of your time and effort. It's very easy once you have the hang of it. Then you can look toward art swaps and engine animations to make it FEEL like things are animated, even though you're not actually creating animated sprite sheets (Hellslave 2's battles are an example of this in action).

comments.author: AliAlHamwi
comments.body:
The messed-up tiles and wrong resolutions are mostly not the generator failing. It's the pipeline asking one MCP chain to both make the art and place it in the scene. Those are different jobs, and when "make a tile and put it in the level" travels through an LLM, the size and position decisions are being made in prose, which is why they come out wrong in ways that feel random.

The split that fixes it: have the generation side write sprites and tiles at fixed native sizes into a folder, and let Godot import from that folder under its own rules. No resolution ever transits through the model. Boring, and it removes exactly the class of mess you're describing.

On the generation side, Ludo.ai also speaks MCP from Cursor or Claude, sprites and sheet animation with a JSON atlas out. I work on Ludo, so that half of the comment is the biased half. The unbiased half is that the pixel artist above has a point, some manual pass survives every tool, and keeping placement in Godot's hands is what makes the manual pass small.
